# SAS for R Programmers {#sec-sas}

R-only graduates of this program have reported being screened out
of industry positions before an interview, because the
application asked for SAS. That failure is at least visible. The
quiet one comes after you are hired. A SAS program and an R
program fit 'the same model' to the same data and report different
numbers. The two languages chose different defaults (a reference
level, a coding scheme, a censoring code, a method for tied event
times), and neither said so. This chapter gives you enough SAS to
read a program and its log, and to move data across the boundary
without losing anything. It also shows how to reproduce the
procedures that fill most clinical study reports. A table lists
the defaults you must set on both sides before the numbers agree.

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*The determined Real Programmer can write FORTRAN programs
in any language.*

[Ed Post]{.smallcaps}, *Real Programmers Don't Use Pascal*
(1983)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::

## Where SAS is required, and where it is not {#sec-sas-when}

A regulatory submission to the United States Food and Drug
Administration (FDA) requires its datasets in SAS XPORT (XPT
version 5) transport format, structured to CDISC (Clinical Data
Interchange Standards Consortium) standards as the FDA Data
Standards Catalog specifies. XPT is an open, documented format
that R writes as readily as SAS does. FDA does not require SAS
software. Its Statistical Software Clarifying Statement (2015)
says sponsors may use any suitable software. R Consortium pilots
have since carried R-based submission packages through FDA review
(@sec-cdisc-industry). Nevertheless, SAS remains the incumbent in
sponsors and contract research organizations (CROs). It is
therefore what most industry teams expect you to read and write.

The division between sectors follows the deliverable rather than
the merits of the languages. Where the deliverable is a regulatory
artifact, changing tools means revalidating a pipeline a regulator
has already accepted. It also means retraining a department
audited on its documented procedures. That cost keeps SAS in most
sponsor-driven trials, much CRO work, and many government
agencies. Where the deliverable is a paper, the ecosystem, cost,
and collaborators favor R. This holds in academic biostatistics,
investigator-initiated trials, cohort epidemiology, and most young
biotechnology companies. Industry positions will expect SAS with R
as a second skill, and academic positions the reverse. A graduate
who reads both is eligible for all of them.

### Getting access

SAS OnDemand for Academics (ODA), at
<https://welcome.oda.sas.com/>, is the free route. It runs SAS
Studio in a browser for students and independent learners. It
needs no installation, and it is enough for every SAS block in
this chapter. Register, note the user ID it assigns (your home
folder is `/home/<user-id>/`), and upload data through the file
pane.[^oda]

[^oda]: As of 2026-10. ODA sessions have memory and storage limits
    (about 5 GB each when last checked) and time out after a period
    of inactivity, so save programs often. SAS University Edition
    was discontinued in 2021. Altair SLC (formerly WPS) is a paid
    third-party implementation that runs most SAS code.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A classmate says R is useless for an FDA submission
because the FDA requires SAS. What is right and wrong in that?

**Answer.** The classmate is wrong about the requirement. The FDA
requires the datasets as XPT version 5 transport files in CDISC
structure. It does not require SAS software, and R writes XPT
(`haven::write_xpt()`, `xportr`). The classmate is right about
the market. Most sponsors and CROs run validated SAS pipelines, so
most industry teams expect you to read and write SAS. The
screening filter reflects that.
:::

## SAS basics for R users {#sec-sas-basics}

### The DATA step and the PROC step

SAS has two constructs, the DATA step and the PROC step. An R
programmer who understands the difference between them has learned
most of what makes the language feel foreign. The difference is in
the unit of computation. R is vectorized: you write an expression
over a whole column. A DATA step reads one observation, runs every
statement against it, writes it out, and loops back for the next.
The loop is implicit, which is why the code looks vectorized when
it is not. Variables persist across statements within a row but
reset between rows. A subsetting `if` discards the observation
rather than returning a filtered copy. `retain` and `lag` exist
because the row-at-a-time model gives no other way to see a
neighboring observation. A PROC step works the other way. It
consumes a whole dataset and produces listings, tables, or
statistical output. An idiomatic program alternates: a DATA step
to shape the data, then a PROC to analyze it.

A DATA step:

```sas
data work.adults;
  set work.demo;
  if age >= 18;
  age_group = ifn(age < 65, 1, 2);
  log_bmi   = log(bmi);
run;
```

In R:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplyr)

demo <- tibble(
  usubjid = sprintf("01-%03d", 1:5),
  age     = c(17, 42, 64, 71, 55),
  sex     = c(1L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 2L),
  bmi     = c(21.4, 27.8, 31.2, 24.9, 29.1)
)

adults <- demo |>
  filter(age >= 18) |>
  mutate(age_group = if_else(age < 65, 1L, 2L),
         log_bmi   = log(bmi))

adults
#> # A tibble: 4 x 6
#>   usubjid   age   sex   bmi age_group log_bmi
#>   <chr>   <dbl> <int> <dbl>     <int>   <dbl>
#> 1 01-002     42     2  27.8         1    3.33
#> 2 01-003     64     2  31.2         1    3.44
#> 3 01-004     71     1  24.9         2    3.21
#> 4 01-005     55     2  29.1         1    3.37
```
:::


And PROC steps on the result. Each procedure has its own syntax.
Most share an `OUT =` option to capture results as a dataset. Most
also use some combination of `BY`, `CLASS`, and `MODEL` statements
to say which variables partition the data and which enter the
analysis.

```sas
proc means data = work.adults n mean std median q1 q3 maxdec = 2;
  class age_group;
  var log_bmi;
run;

proc freq data = work.adults;
  tables age_group * sex / chisq;
run;
```

### Libraries and formats

A library (`libname`) is a directory of SAS datasets. Datasets in
`WORK`, the temporary library, vanish at the end of the session;
named libraries persist.

```sas
libname mylib '/home/u99999999/data';
data mylib.demo_archive;
  set work.demo;
run;
```

A format controls how a value displays (`1` as `'Male'`). An
informat controls how input is read. `PROC FORMAT` defines them.
The R analog is a factor with explicit labels:

```sas
proc format;
  value sexfmt 1 = 'Male' 2 = 'Female';
run;

data work.demo2;
  set work.demo;
  format sex sexfmt.;
run;
```

Six procedures cover most data-cleaning code you will read:
`PROC SORT` (`arrange()`), `PROC PRINT` (`head()`),
`PROC CONTENTS` (`str()`, `glimpse()`), `PROC FREQ` (`count()`,
`table()`), `PROC MEANS` (`summary()`, `summarize()`), and
`PROC UNIVARIATE` (`quantile()` and distribution summaries).

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**In SAS, a missing number is smaller than every number.** The
subsetting `if age < 18;` keeps subjects whose age is missing,
because SAS compares a missing value as lower than any value. In
R, `filter(age < 18)` drops them, because the comparison is `NA`.
The same condition therefore selects different subjects in the two
languages, with no message in either. Test for missing values
explicitly on both sides (`if not missing(age) and age < 18;`).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** In a DATA step, `total = total + dose;` leaves
`total` missing on every row. Why, and what is the R analog of the
fix?

**Answer.** A DATA step resets non-retained variables to missing at
the start of each row. `total` is therefore missing when the
statement runs, and missing plus a number is missing.
`retain total 0;` keeps the running value across rows, as does the
sum statement `total + dose;`, which retains implicitly. In R the
whole computation is one vectorized call, `cumsum(dose)`, usually
within `group_by()`.
:::

## Procedures and the defaults that differ {#sec-sas-procs}

### Procedure correspondence

The R-to-SAS map for the procedures a clinical biostatistician uses
most is in @tbl-sas-procs.

| R | SAS |
|---|---|
| `head(df)` | `PROC PRINT DATA = df (OBS = 10);` |
| `str(df)` | `PROC CONTENTS DATA = df;` |
| `summary(df$x)` | `PROC MEANS DATA = df N MEAN STD;` |
| `table(df$x, df$y)` | `PROC FREQ DATA = df; TABLES x*y;` |
| `t.test(y ~ g, data = df)` | `PROC TTEST DATA = df; CLASS g; VAR y;` |
| `lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = df)` | `PROC REG DATA = df; MODEL y = x1 x2;` |
| `aov(y ~ g, data = df)` | `PROC GLM DATA = df; CLASS g; MODEL y = g;` |
| `glm(y ~ x, family = binomial)` | `PROC LOGISTIC DATA = df; MODEL y (EVENT = '1') = x;` |
| `glm(y ~ x, family = poisson)` | `PROC GENMOD DATA = df; MODEL y = x / DIST = POISSON LINK = LOG;` |
| `lme4::lmer(y ~ x + (1 \| id))` | `PROC MIXED DATA = df; CLASS id; MODEL y = x; RANDOM INTERCEPT / SUBJECT = id;` |
| `mmrm::mmrm(y ~ x * v + us(v \| id))` | `PROC MIXED; CLASS id v; MODEL y = x v x*v; REPEATED v / SUBJECT = id TYPE = UN;` |
| `survfit(Surv(t, e) ~ g)` | `PROC LIFETEST DATA = df; TIME t*c(1); STRATA g;` |
| `coxph(Surv(t, e) ~ x)` | `PROC PHREG DATA = df; MODEL t*c(1) = x;` |

: R functions and their SAS procedures. In the survival rows, `e`
is an event indicator and `c` a censoring indicator. {#tbl-sas-procs}

### `PROC GLM` and estimated marginal means

```sas
proc glm data = work.penguins;
  class species;
  model body_mass_g = species flipper_length_mm;
  lsmeans species / pdiff cl;
run;
quit;
```

R equivalent:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(palmerpenguins)
penguins_clean <- na.omit(penguins)

fit <- lm(body_mass_g ~ species + flipper_length_mm,
          data = penguins_clean)
emmeans::emmeans(fit, "species", contr = "pairwise",
                 infer = TRUE)
#> $emmeans
#>  species   emmean   SE  df lower.CL upper.CL t.ratio p.value
#>  Adelie      4147 45.5 329     4058     4237  91.073 <0.0001
#>  Chinstrap   3942 48.0 329     3848     4036  82.195 <0.0001
#>  Gentoo      4432 60.7 329     4312     4551  73.048 <0.0001
#> 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95 
#> 
#> $contrasts
#>  contrast           estimate   SE  df lower.CL upper.CL t.ratio p.value
#>  Adelie - Chinstrap      205 57.6 329     69.8    340.9   3.568  0.0012
#>  Adelie - Gentoo        -285 95.4 329   -509.2    -59.8  -2.981  0.0086
#>  Chinstrap - Gentoo     -490 87.0 329   -694.7   -285.1  -5.631 <0.0001
#> 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95 
#> Conf-level adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 3 estimates 
#> P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 3 estimates
```
:::


The `lsmeans` statement produces estimated marginal means
(least-squares means). The `emmeans` package is the R counterpart.
Marginal means do not depend on which level is the reference,
which makes them the right quantities to compare across the two
languages. The coefficients do depend on it. `PROC GLM` uses a
less-than-full-rank parameterization whose `solution` reports each
`species` level against the *last* sorted level (Gentoo). By
contrast, `lm()` reports each against the *first* (Adelie). The
`flipper_length_mm` slope, the overall fit, and the fitted values
match exactly. To make the `species` rows match term for term,
relevel in R with `relevel(species, ref = 'Gentoo')`.

### `PROC LOGISTIC` and reference coding

```sas
proc logistic data = work.trial;
  class treatment (param = ref ref = 'placebo')
        sex (param = ref ref = 'M');
  model outcome (event = '1') = treatment age sex;
  oddsratio treatment;
run;
```

R equivalent:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(4)
n <- 200
trial <- data.frame(
  treatment = rep(c("placebo", "active"), each = n / 2),
  age       = round(rnorm(n, 62, 9)),
  sex       = sample(c("M", "F"), n, replace = TRUE),
  outcome   = rbinom(n, 1, 0.3)
)

trial$treatment <- relevel(factor(trial$treatment),
                           ref = "placebo")
trial$sex <- relevel(factor(trial$sex), ref = "M")
fit <- glm(outcome ~ treatment + age + sex,
           family = binomial, data = trial)
broom::tidy(fit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 7
#>   term            estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high
#>   <chr>              <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept)        0.136    1.21      -1.64    0.101   0.0120      1.43
#> 2 treatmentactive    0.827    0.320     -0.592   0.554   0.439       1.55
#> 3 age                1.02     0.0185     0.945   0.344   0.982       1.06
#> 4 sexF               1.11     0.322      0.334   0.738   0.591       2.10
```
:::


Three settings in the SAS code exist only to match R. First,
`param = ref` requests reference coding, which is R's default.
Without it, `PROC LOGISTIC` uses effect coding (sum-to-zero),
whose coefficients are deviations from the average over levels.
Second, `ref =` names the reference level. SAS otherwise takes the
*last* level in sort order and R the *first*. For `active` and
`placebo`, the defaults therefore pick opposite references and
report the same effect with opposite signs. Third, `event = '1'`
makes SAS model the probability that `outcome` is 1. By default
`PROC LOGISTIC` models the lowest ordered value, here 0, which
flips the sign of every coefficient. `PROC GENMOD` defaults
instead to the less-than-full-rank `PARAM = GLM` coding. That
coding behaves like reference coding with the last level as
reference. `PROC GLM` and `PROC MIXED` use their own
less-than-full-rank coding and do not take `param =`.

### The defaults that differ

@tbl-sas-defaults collects the defaults that make an R fit and a
SAS fit of 'the same model' disagree. Each is silent. Both
programs run and print a plausible table.

| Setting | R default | SAS default | Set both sides to |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reference level of a categorical predictor | First level (alphabetical unless set) | Last level in sort order | `relevel(x, ref =)`; `CLASS x (REF = '...')` |
| Coding of a categorical predictor | Reference (treatment) contrasts | `LOGISTIC`: effect coding; `GENMOD`: `PARAM = GLM`; `GLM`, `MIXED`: less-than-full-rank | `PARAM = REF`, or compare marginal means |
| Modeled outcome in logistic regression | `P(y = 1)` (the second factor level) | The lowest ordered value, `P(y = 0)` | `MODEL y (EVENT = '1') =` |
| Mixed-model covariance | `lmer()`: random effects only; `mmrm()`: the structure in the formula | `RANDOM`: variance components (`VC`); `REPEATED` needs `TYPE =` | `TYPE = UN` with `us()`, or the same named structure |
| Denominator degrees of freedom | `lmer()`: none; `mmrm()`: Satterthwaite | Containment or between-within, by statement | `method = "Kenward-Roger"`; `DDFM = KR` |
| Tied event times in a Cox model | Efron | Breslow | `ties = "breslow"`, or `TIES = EFRON` |
| Confidence interval for a survival curve | Log (`conf.type = "log"`) | Log-log (`CONFTYPE = LOGLOG`) | Either, stated |
| Censoring indicator | `Surv(t, e)`: `e = 1` is an event | `TIME t*c(list)`: values in the list are censored | CDISC: `Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0)`; `aval*cnsr(1 2)` |
| Missing value in a comparison | `NA`; `filter()` drops the row | Smaller than any number; `x < 5` is true | Test `missing()` and `is.na()` explicitly |
| Date origin | 1970-01-01 | 1960-01-01 | `as.Date(x, origin = "1960-01-01")` for bare numbers |
| Sums of squares in ANOVA | `anova()`: sequential (Type I) | `PROC GLM` prints Type I and Type III | `car::Anova(type = 3)` with sum contrasts |

: Defaults that differ between R and SAS. Set every row
explicitly in both programs before comparing numbers.
{#tbl-sas-defaults}

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
Use a model to translate between the languages, with the defaults
table as the acceptance criteria.

> **Context.** Below is an R analysis I need reproduced in SAS for
> a CRO validation: [the R code, and the variable names and types
> of the input dataset; no data rows].
>
> **Constraints.** Write SAS 9.4 code using `PROC LOGISTIC` (or
> the procedure I name). Set the reference level of every `CLASS`
> variable with `PARAM = REF` and `REF =`, state `EVENT =` for the
> modeled outcome, and for any survival model state `TIES =` and
> list every censoring code in `TIME aval*cnsr(...)`.
>
> **Criteria.** For each row of this table [paste
> @tbl-sas-defaults], say which line of your code sets it, or why
> it does not apply. Name the output table (`ODS OUTPUT`) whose
> estimates I should compare with `broom::tidy()` in R.

*Failure mode.* Models translate the syntax and leave the defaults
unchanged. The result has no `EVENT =`, no `REF =`, and Breslow
ties against R's Efron. For survival models, the event and
censoring codes are often confused. In R's `Surv()`, a status of 1
marks an event. SAS's `TIME aval*cnsr(1)` lists the values that
mark *censoring*. The CDISC `CNSR` variable codes 0 as the event.
A model that writes `aval*cnsr(0)` for an ADaM dataset has
inverted the analysis. *Check.* Run both programs on the same data
and compare estimates to four decimal places. Trace any
disagreement to a row of @tbl-sas-defaults before accepting
either.
:::

### A side-by-side example

A penguin model in both languages:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + species,
          data = na.omit(penguins))
broom::tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 7
#>   term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
#>   <chr>                <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept)        -4013.     586.       -6.85 3.74e-11  -5166.    -2860. 
#> 2 flipper_length_mm     40.6      3.08     13.2  3.64e-32     34.5      46.7
#> 3 speciesChinstrap    -205.      57.6      -3.57 4.14e- 4   -319.      -92.1
#> 4 speciesGentoo        285.      95.4       2.98 3.08e- 3     96.8     472.
```
:::


```sas
proc import datafile = '/home/u99999999/penguins.csv'
            out = work.penguins dbms = csv replace;
  getnames = yes;
run;

data work.penguins_clean;
  set work.penguins;
  if cmiss(of _all_) = 0;
run;

proc glm data = work.penguins_clean;
  class species;
  model body_mass_g = flipper_length_mm species / clparm solution;
run;
quit;
```

The slope, the overall fit, and the fitted values agree. The
`species` rows differ by reference level, as in the `PROC GLM`
example above. One more difference can hide in the import. R's
`read.csv()` reads the text `NA` as missing. `PROC IMPORT` treats
it as an ordinary value and may read a numeric column that
contains it as character. As a result, `cmiss()` may count
different rows as complete. Compare the number of observations
used before comparing estimates.

### Exercises

These need no SAS. Predict first, then check the prediction in R.

1. A SAS programmer fits
   `proc logistic data = adsl; class trt01p sex; model event30 = trt01p age sex; run;`
   on the HF-HOME `ADSL` joined to the 30-day outcome, with no
   options. You fit `glm(event30 ~ TRT01P + AGE + SEX, binomial)`
   with R's defaults. Predict, for the `AGE` coefficient and the
   treatment coefficient, how the two will differ. Then reproduce
   the SAS defaults in R to confirm.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
Three defaults differ. First, SAS models `P(event30 = 0)`, the
lowest ordered value, so every coefficient changes sign. Second,
SAS uses effect coding. A two-level `CLASS` variable gets one
column coded `+1` and `-1`, and its coefficient is half the
difference between the levels. Third, SAS sorts `trt01p` levels
alphabetically (`'Home health'` before `'Usual care'`), as R does,
but codes the first level `+1`. The prediction is as follows.
SAS's `AGE` coefficient is the negative of R's. SAS's treatment
coefficient is half of R's `TRT01PUsual care` coefficient, with
the same sign. R reproduces SAS's defaults with `contr.sum` and
the outcome reversed:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
source(file.path("..", "..", "R", "hfhome.R"))
hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
outcomes <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(hf_dir, "outcomes.csv"),
  col_types = readr::cols(patient_id = "c", .default = "?"))

lr_data <- hfhome_sdtm()$dm |>
  transmute(USUBJID, TRT01P = ARM, AGE, SEX) |>
  inner_join(transmute(outcomes,
                       USUBJID = paste("HFHOME", patient_id,
                                       sep = "-"),
                       event30 = event_30d),
             by = "USUBJID", relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  filter(!is.na(event30)) |>
  mutate(TRT01P = factor(TRT01P), SEX = factor(SEX))

r_fit <- glm(event30 ~ TRT01P + AGE + SEX, family = binomial,
             data = lr_data)
sas_like <- glm(I(1 - event30) ~ TRT01P + AGE + SEX,
                family = binomial, data = lr_data,
                contrasts = list(TRT01P = "contr.sum",
                                 SEX = "contr.sum"))

rbind(r = coef(r_fit), sas_defaults = coef(sas_like))
#>              (Intercept) TRT01PUsual care         AGE       SEXM
#> r              -3.066234       0.14758053  0.02280302 0.17502248
#> sas_defaults    2.904932       0.07379026 -0.02280302 0.08751124
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(coef(sas_like)[["AGE"]], -coef(r_fit)[["AGE"]])),
  isTRUE(all.equal(coef(sas_like)[["TRT01P1"]],
                   coef(r_fit)[["TRT01PUsual care"]] / 2))
)
```
:::


This reproduces what SAS's defaults imply, by construction. It is
not a SAS run. SAS's log would say which outcome it modeled
('Probability modeled is event30=0.'). That is the line to look
for when two answers have opposite signs.
:::

2. Fit the Cox model of HF-HOME's `ADTTE` (time to readmission or
   death by randomized arm) in R twice, once with R's default
   handling of tied event times and once with SAS's. Predict
   whether the hazard ratios differ in the second decimal place.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
The prediction is as follows. Times are recorded in whole days, so
many events are tied. Breslow's approximation pulls the
coefficient toward zero relative to Efron's. With about a fifth of
subjects having an event, the approximation error is small. We
expect agreement to two decimal places and a difference in the
third or fourth.




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
efron   <- coxph(Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0) ~ TRT01P, data = adtte)
breslow <- coxph(Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0) ~ TRT01P, data = adtte,
                 ties = "breslow")
round(c(efron = exp(coef(efron)), breslow = exp(coef(breslow))), 4)
#>   efron.TRT01PHome health breslow.TRT01PHome health 
#>                    0.8517                    0.8525
```
:::


The two hazard ratios differ by
0.0007.
That is too little to change any conclusion, but enough to fail a
validation that compares results to four decimal places.
`PROC PHREG` without `TIES = EFRON` reproduces the second number,
not the first. Neither is wrong. The specification should name
one, and both programs should use it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You translate a logistic regression from R to SAS,
set `param = ref`, and the treatment coefficient now has the same
magnitude as R's but the opposite sign. Name the two settings that
could each explain it.

**Answer.** The first is the reference level. SAS takes the last
level and R the first, so `ref =` must name the same level on both
sides. The second is the modeled outcome. SAS models the lowest
ordered value unless `event = '1'`. Either alone flips the sign,
and both together flip it back. That is why a sign that agrees is
not evidence that the settings do.
:::

## Mixed models and MMRM in both languages {#sec-sas-mixed}

### A random intercept

```sas
proc mixed data = work.long covtest;
  class subject visit treatment;
  model y = treatment visit treatment*visit / solution;
  random intercept / subject = subject;
run;
```

R equivalent:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(lme4)

set.seed(5)
subject_effect <- rnorm(40, 0, 1.5)

# treatment is assigned per subject, so it is constant within
# subject, as in a parallel-group trial
long <- expand.grid(subject = factor(1:40), visit = factor(1:3)) |>
  mutate(
    treatment = if_else(as.integer(subject) <= 20,
                        "placebo", "active"),
    treatment = relevel(factor(treatment), ref = "placebo"),
    y = 10 + 2 * (treatment == "active") +
        0.5 * as.integer(visit) +
        subject_effect[as.integer(subject)] +
        rnorm(n(), 0, 2)
  )

stopifnot(all(tapply(long$treatment, long$subject,
                     \(x) length(unique(x))) == 1))

fit <- lmer(y ~ treatment * visit + (1 | subject), data = long)
summary(fit)$coefficients
#>                          Estimate Std. Error    t value
#> (Intercept)            10.3179110  0.5784227 17.8380125
#> treatmentactive         2.3571550  0.8180132  2.8815611
#> visit2                  0.5167972  0.5741178  0.9001588
#> visit3                  0.5467634  0.5741178  0.9523541
#> treatmentactive:visit2  0.5133472  0.8119251  0.6322593
#> treatmentactive:visit3  1.1889715  0.8119251  1.4643856
```
:::


Both fit the same model. `visit` is categorical on both sides
(`CLASS` in SAS, a factor in R), and both estimate by REML
(restricted maximum likelihood). The fixed-effect tables still
differ term for term. `PROC MIXED` zeroes the *last* level of each
`CLASS` variable (visit 3, and `placebo`, which sorts after
`active`), while R zeroes the first. Placebo is the reference on
both sides. For `visit`, compare fitted means (`LSMEANS` in SAS,
`emmeans` in R) rather than coefficients. `PROC MIXED`'s default
covariance for a `RANDOM` statement is variance components
(`VC`). For a random intercept, that matches `lme4`'s default. A
random slope with an unstructured covariance needs
`random intercept visit / subject = subject type = un;`.

### MMRM: a mixed model for repeated measures

The primary analysis of a continuous endpoint measured at
scheduled visits in a trial is usually an MMRM. Visit, treatment,
and their interaction enter as fixed effects. There are no random
effects at all. Instead, an unstructured covariance links a
subject's visits, so that each visit has its own variance and each
pair its own correlation. In SAS this is `PROC MIXED` with a
`REPEATED` statement. In R it is the `mmrm` package
[@sabanesbove2026mmrm], written by an industry working group to
reproduce SAS's results.

```sas
proc mixed data = work.long method = reml;
  class subject visit treatment;
  model y = treatment visit treatment*visit / ddfm = kr solution;
  repeated visit / subject = subject type = un;
  lsmeans treatment*visit / diff cl;
run;
```

R equivalent:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(mmrm)

fit_mmrm <- mmrm(y ~ treatment * visit + us(visit | subject),
                 data = long, method = "Kenward-Roger")
emmeans::emmeans(fit_mmrm, ~ treatment | visit) |>
  pairs(reverse = TRUE)
#> visit = 1:
#>  contrast         estimate    SE df t.ratio p.value
#>  active - placebo     2.36 0.660 38   3.571  0.0010
#> 
#> visit = 2:
#>  contrast         estimate    SE df t.ratio p.value
#>  active - placebo     2.87 0.841 38   3.414  0.0015
#> 
#> visit = 3:
#>  contrast         estimate    SE df t.ratio p.value
#>  active - placebo     3.55 0.884 38   4.013  0.0003
```
:::


The two sides agree on the fitted model only because three
settings were made to agree. These are the covariance (`TYPE = UN`
and `us()`), the estimation method (REML in both), and the
denominator degrees of freedom (`DDFM = KR` and
`method = "Kenward-Roger"`). If you leave out `DDFM = KR`, SAS
uses the between-within method. With `TYPE = UN` and no `RANDOM`
statement, that method gives every effect the between-subject
degrees of freedom. If you leave out `method =`, `mmrm` uses
Satterthwaite's. The estimates agree either way. The confidence
intervals and p-values do not.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Without SAS, check the MMRM against an independent R
implementation of the same model: generalized least squares with
an unstructured correlation and a separate variance per visit.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_gls <- nlme::gls(
  y ~ treatment * visit, data = long, method = "REML",
  correlation = nlme::corSymm(form = ~ as.integer(visit) | subject),
  weights = nlme::varIdent(form = ~ 1 | visit)
)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(coef(fit_mmrm), coef(fit_gls),
                           tolerance = 1e-4)))
cbind(mmrm = coef(fit_mmrm), gls = coef(fit_gls))
#>                              mmrm        gls
#> (Intercept)            10.3179110 10.3179110
#> treatmentactive         2.3571550  2.3571550
#> visit2                  0.5167972  0.5167972
#> visit3                  0.5467634  0.5467634
#> treatmentactive:visit2  0.5133472  0.5133472
#> treatmentactive:visit3  1.1889715  1.1889715
```
:::


Agreement between two R packages is evidence that `mmrm` fit the
model you specified. Agreement with SAS still has to be checked
on SAS output, against the same three settings.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Your R MMRM and a colleague's `PROC MIXED` give the
same treatment difference at the last visit but different
confidence intervals. The SAS code has `repeated visit / subject =
subject type = un;` and no `DDFM =`. What do you change?

**Answer.** The degrees of freedom. Without `DDFM =`, a model with
only a `REPEATED` statement uses the between-within method. Your
`mmrm` fit used Kenward-Roger or Satterthwaite. Add `DDFM = KR` in
SAS (or choose the same method in `mmrm`), and the intervals
should then agree. Equal estimates with unequal intervals point at
the degrees of freedom or the covariance structure, not the mean
model.
:::

## Survival analysis on the HF-HOME ADTTE {#sec-sas-survival}

This section reuses the HF-HOME `ADSL` and `ADTTE` built in
@sec-cdisc-worked. The chunk that rebuilds them here is hidden. It
repeats the derivation of that section, so that this chapter
renders on its own.



The SAS side reads `adtte.xpt`, written from R in
@sec-sas-transport. `CNSR` takes the values 1 (no event by day 30)
and 2 (lost to follow-up), so the censoring list names both:

```sas
proc lifetest data = work.adtte plots = survival(atrisk);
  where ittfl = 'Y';
  time aval * cnsr(1 2);
  strata trt01p;
run;

proc phreg data = work.adtte;
  where ittfl = 'Y';
  class trt01p (param = ref ref = 'Usual care')
        sex    (param = ref ref = 'F');
  model aval * cnsr(1 2) = trt01p age sex / ties = efron risklimits;
run;
```

R equivalent:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
analysis <- filter(adtte, ITTFL == "Y")

fit_km <- survfit(Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0) ~ TRT01P, data = analysis)
fit_cox <- coxph(Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0) ~ TRT01P + AGE + SEX,
                 data = analysis)
fit_cox
#> Call:
#> coxph(formula = Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0) ~ TRT01P + AGE + SEX, data = analysis)
#> 
#>                        coef exp(coef)  se(coef)      z        p
#> TRT01PHome health -0.165974  0.847068  0.088947 -1.866   0.0620
#> AGE                0.019674  1.019869  0.004161  4.728 2.27e-06
#> SEXM               0.156244  1.169112  0.090363  1.729   0.0838
#> 
#> Likelihood ratio test=28.17  on 3 df, p=3.338e-06
#> n= 2432, number of events= 508
stopifnot(fit_cox$n == nrow(analysis))
```
:::


Each line of the SAS code answers a row of @tbl-sas-defaults.
`cnsr(1 2)` lists every censoring value, the counterpart of R's
`CNSR == 0`. `ties = efron` matches `coxph()`. `ref = 'Usual care'`
matches the factor level order set in `ADSL`. Finally, `sex`
appears in the `CLASS` statement because `PROC PHREG` stops with
an error on a character variable in `MODEL` that is not declared
there. Its reference, `'F'`, is the level R chooses by default
(first alphabetically).

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**`time aval*cnsr(1)` on a dataset with `CNSR = 2` counts the
lost-to-follow-up subjects as events.** SAS treats every value not
in the list as an event, so the 163 HF-HOME subjects lost to
follow-up would become early events, at their last contact, with
no message.
List every censoring code the dataset contains, and check the
event count in the `PROC LIFETEST` summary against
`sum(CNSR == 0)`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** The `PROC PHREG` output reports 671 events; R's
`coxph()` reports 508 on the same file. Which line of the SAS code
do you check first?

**Answer.** The `MODEL` statement's censoring list. 671 is 508
plus the 163 subjects lost to follow-up. That is what
`aval*cnsr(1)` produces when `CNSR` also takes the value 2. A
difference in the event count is always a data or coding
difference, never a default of the estimator. Check it before
comparing any estimate.
:::

## Reading SAS logs {#sec-sas-logs}

SAS writes three tiers of message to the log:

- **ERROR**: the step stopped. Fix and rerun.
- **WARNING**: something unexpected happened and the program
  continued. Always inspect.
- **NOTE**: information about what the program did. Most are
  benign; a few report lost or multiplied data, and SAS does not
  flag them.

### An annotated log

The log below is from a DATA step that merges a demographics file
with a visits file (display-only; constructed for this chapter,
not produced by a SAS run). The annotations mark what to read.

```
1    data work.analytic;
2      merge work.demo work.visits;
3      by patient_id;
4      pulse_pressure = sbp - dbp;
5      sbp_high = (sbp > 140);
6    run;

WARNING: Multiple lengths were specified for the BY variable   (1)
         patient_id by input data sets. This might cause
         unexpected results.
NOTE: MERGE statement has more than one data set with repeats  (2)
      of BY values.
NOTE: Missing values were generated as a result of performing  (3)
      an operation on missing values.
      Each place is given by: (Number of times) at
      (Line):(Column).
      41 at 4:24
NOTE: There were 2432 observations read from the data set
      WORK.DEMO.
NOTE: There were 6317 observations read from the data set
      WORK.VISITS.
NOTE: The data set WORK.ANALYTIC has 6330 observations and 12  (4)
      variables.
```

1. The `BY` variable has different lengths in the two inputs, for
   example `$4` in one and `$8` in the other. Values can be
   truncated or fail to match, so some subjects may not merge.
   Make the lengths equal before the merge.
2. Both datasets have more than one row for some `patient_id`.
   Within such a group, `MERGE` pairs rows one to one in order and
   repeats the last row of the shorter dataset. It does not form
   every combination as an SQL join would. The result is wrong,
   and the step 'completes'. A demographics file should have one
   row per patient, so this NOTE means it does not.
3. The subtraction on line 4 met a missing `sbp` or `dbp` 41
   times. Line 5 compared the same missing values with 140 and
   produced no message at all. A missing value is smaller than any
   number, so `sbp_high` is 0, not missing, and those visits are
   counted as not high. The NOTE on line 4 is the only sign of the
   silent comparison on line 5.
4. More rows than either input. Without `IN=` flags, `MERGE` is a
   full outer join that keeps unmatched rows from both datasets.
   The count can therefore rise from unmatched keys as well as
   from repeats. 6,330 against 6,317 visits means 13 rows to
   account for.

Read the log end to end after every run, not only the last lines.
For automated checking, `PROC SQL` can assert a row count and
write an `ERROR` line that log scanners catch:

```sas
proc sql noprint;
  select count(*) into :n_visits from work.visits;
  select count(*) into :n_merged from work.analytic;
quit;
%if &n_visits ne &n_merged %then %do;
  %put ERROR: Merge changed the row count: &n_visits -> &n_merged;
%end;
```

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
> **Context.** Below is the complete log of a SAS program that
> merges and derives an analysis dataset, with patient
> identifiers replaced by synthetic values: [log]. The program
> should produce one row per visit from a demographics file with
> one row per patient.
>
> **Constraints.** Do not rewrite the program yet.
>
> **Criteria.** List every ERROR, every WARNING, and every NOTE
> that could indicate lost, multiplied, truncated, or silently
> missing data, quoting the line. For each, say what in the data
> would produce it and what check would confirm it.

*Failure mode.* Models explain the ERRORs well and pass over the
NOTEs, which is where the merge and missing-value problems are.
They also suggest suppressing a WARNING rather than finding its
cause. *Check.* Confirm each flagged message against the data (a
`count()` of duplicated keys, a comparison of variable lengths with
`PROC CONTENTS`). Fix the cause, rerun, and require a log with no
WARNING and no merge or missing-value NOTE. Logs can contain data
values, so replace identifiers before sending one
(@sec-ai-governance).
:::

### Exercises

3. Read this log (display-only; constructed for the exercise) and
   say what happened, how many records it affected, and what you
   would change.

   ```
   NOTE: Character values have been converted to numeric values
         at the places given by: (Line):(Column).
         14:12
   NOTE: Invalid numeric data, sbp_discharge='NA' , at line 14
         column 12.
   NOTE: Missing values were generated as a result of performing
         an operation on missing values.
         Each place is given by: (Number of times) at
         (Line):(Column).
         78 at 15:20
   NOTE: There were 2432 observations read from the data set
         WORK.CRF.
   NOTE: The data set WORK.CRF2 has 2432 observations and 9
         variables.
   ```

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
`sbp_discharge` arrived as character, and line 14 used it in a
numeric expression, so SAS converted it implicitly. The text `'NA'`
(and any other non-numeric code) became missing, with an 'Invalid
numeric data' note for each such value. SAS prints only the first
several of these notes, so the log does not say how many there
were. Line 15 then produced missing results 78 times, which is the
affected count for that expression. The row count is unchanged,
which is why the step looks fine.

The fix is to convert deliberately. Read the column as character,
and recode the site's missing-value codes (`'NA'`, `'-99'`, empty)
to missing explicitly. Then convert with
`input(sbp_discharge, best.)` and count the missing values before
and after. HF-HOME's `crf_export.csv` uses exactly these codes;
@sec-missing gives the R side.
:::

4. A colleague's log ends with
   `NOTE: The data set WORK.ADSL has 2432 observations and 40 variables.`
   and contains no ERROR or WARNING. They conclude the merge that
   built it was correct. Name two problems this log cannot rule
   out, and the check for each.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
A count equal to the number of subjects rules out neither of the
failures @sec-joins describes. First, some subjects may have
failed to match. A full outer `MERGE` without `IN=` keeps them,
with missing values in the other dataset's variables. Second, a
repeated key may have been paired row by row and replaced a
correct value with a wrong one, which leaves the count unchanged.
For the first, count missing values in a variable that comes from
each input (`PROC MEANS NMISS` or `PROC FREQ`). For the second,
confirm one row per key in each input before the merge
(`PROC SORT NODUPKEY` into a separate dataset and compare counts,
or `PROC SQL` with `GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`). The
absence of a WARNING is not evidence, because the repeats NOTE is
a NOTE.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Why does the book treat `NOTE: MERGE statement has
more than one data set with repeats of BY values` as more
dangerous than most ERRORs?

**Answer.** An ERROR stops the step, so nothing downstream runs on
its output. The repeats NOTE lets the step finish and produce a
dataset with the expected columns and a plausible row count, built
from mismatched rows. It is the SAS form of the many-to-many join
of @sec-joins, without the warning `dplyr` gives.
:::

## Moving data between SAS and R {#sec-sas-transport}

A mixed-language project tends to go wrong at the boundary between
the languages. @fig-sas-boundary marks it, with the properties to
check every time something crosses.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-sas-boundary
%%| fig-alt: "Left-to-right round trip. R cleans and derives, then
%%|   writes a version 5 transport file with haven::write_xpt. SAS
%%|   reads it through libname xport and proc copy, analyzes, and
%%|   writes a second transport file, which R reads back with
%%|   haven::read_xpt to tabulate and plot. A separate node points
%%|   by dashed arrows at both transport files, requiring a check of
%%|   row count, variable names, types and labels at each
%%|   crossing."
%%| fig-cap: "The R and SAS boundary. Transport version 5 is the
%%|   durable interchange format and the one the FDA requires. Each
%%|   crossing is a place where variable names can be truncated,
%%|   types can change, and labels can be lost, so each crossing
%%|   deserves an explicit check rather than an assumption."
flowchart LR
  R1["<b>R</b><br/><i>clean, derive</i>"]
  R1 -->|"haven::write_xpt<br/>version = 5"| X1[".xpt"]
  X1 -->|"libname xport<br/>proc copy"| S["<b>SAS</b><br/><i>analyze, ODS output</i>"]
  S -->|"libname out xport"| X2[".xpt"]
  X2 -->|"haven::read_xpt"| R2["<b>R</b><br/><i>tabulate, plot</i>"]
  C["<b>Check at every crossing</b><br/><i>row count, variable names,<br/>types and labels</i>"] -.-> X1
  C -.-> X2
```

### R to SAS

XPT version 5 allows variable names of at most eight characters
and has no factor type. `haven::write_xpt()` handles both without
an error, in ways you need to know. It truncates a longer name to
eight characters, so two names that share their first eight
collide. It also writes a factor as its integer codes, so `TRT01P`
arrives in SAS as 1 and 2. Convert factors to character and check
name lengths before writing:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(haven)

xpt_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "xpt")
dir.create(xpt_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

adtte_out <- adtte |>
  mutate(TRT01P = as.character(TRT01P))
attr(adtte_out$AVAL, "label") <- "Analysis Value (days)"
attr(adtte_out$CNSR, "label") <- "Censor (0 = event)"

stopifnot(all(nchar(names(adtte_out)) <= 8),
          !any(vapply(adtte_out, is.factor, logical(1))))
write_xpt(adtte_out, file.path(xpt_dir, "adtte.xpt"),
          version = 5, name = "ADTTE")
```
:::


In SAS:

```sas
libname x xport '/home/u99999999/adtte.xpt';
proc copy in = x out = work; run;
libname x clear;
```

### SAS to R, and the round trip

`haven::read_xpt()` and `haven::read_sas()` (for `.sas7bdat`)
bring SAS data back. They keep each variable's label as an
attribute and convert variables that carry a SAS date format to
`Date`. SAS stores a date as days since 1 January 1960, and R
counts from 1 January 1970. A date that arrives as a bare number,
without a format, is therefore ten years wrong unless converted
with `as.Date(x, origin = "1960-01-01")`.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Read the transport file back and compare it with what was written:
row count, names, types, labels, dates, and values.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
back <- read_xpt(file.path(xpt_dir, "adtte.xpt"))

stopifnot(
  nrow(back) == nrow(adtte_out),
  identical(names(back), names(adtte_out)),
  inherits(back$ADT, "Date"),
  identical(attr(back$AVAL, "label"), "Analysis Value (days)"),
  isTRUE(all.equal(as.data.frame(zap_labels(back)),
                   as.data.frame(zap_labels(adtte_out)),
                   check.attributes = FALSE))
)
str(back[c("USUBJID", "TRT01P", "ADT", "AVAL", "CNSR")])
#> tibble [2,432 x 5] (S3: tbl_df/tbl/data.frame)
#>  $ USUBJID: chr [1:2432] "HFHOME-0001" "HFHOME-0002" "HFHOME-0003" "HFHOME-0004" ...
#>  $ TRT01P : chr [1:2432] "Home health" "Home health" "Usual care" "Usual care" ...
#>  $ ADT    : Date[1:2432], format: "2024-03-02" "2024-03-02" ...
#>  $ AVAL   : num [1:2432] 30 30 30 30 30 30 30 30 30 18 ...
#>   ..- attr(*, "label")= chr "Analysis Value (days)"
#>  $ CNSR   : num [1:2432] 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 ...
#>   ..- attr(*, "label")= chr "Censor (0 = event)"
```
:::


`CNSR` comes back as a double, because XPT stores every number as
one. `all.equal()` compares values, so that change passes, and it
is harmless. `TRT01P` comes back as character with its levels in
no particular order. Set the reference level again before fitting
anything (@tbl-sas-defaults).
:::

For workflows in which R prepares the data, SAS fits the models,
and R produces the tables, SAS writes its results to a second
transport file through ODS (display-only):

```sas
proc phreg data = work.adtte;
  where ittfl = 'Y';
  class trt01p (param = ref ref = 'Usual care');
  model aval * cnsr(1 2) = trt01p / ties = efron risklimits;
  ods output ParameterEstimates = pe;
run;

libname out xport '/home/u99999999/results.xpt';
data out.pe;
  set pe(keep = Parameter Estimate StdErr HazardRatio
         rename = (HazardRatio = HR));
run;
libname out clear;
```

`HazardRatio` is renamed because version 5 names are limited to
eight characters. The R side reads the file and builds the table.
Below, a file written from R's own fit stands in for the one SAS
would write, so that the R side runs here.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
cox_itt <- coxph(Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0) ~ TRT01P, data = analysis)
results_path <- file.path(xpt_dir, "results.xpt")
write_xpt(
  data.frame(Parameter = "TRT01P",
             Estimate  = unname(coef(cox_itt)),
             StdErr    = unname(sqrt(diag(vcov(cox_itt)))),
             HR        = unname(exp(coef(cox_itt)))),
  results_path, version = 5)

results <- read_xpt(results_path)
gt::gt(results) |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns = c(Estimate, StdErr, HR), decimals = 3)
```

Paramete & Estimate & StdErr & HR \\ 
\midrule\addlinespace[2.5pt]
TRT01P & -0.160 & 0.089 & 0.852 \\ 
\bottomrule
\end{tabular*}
\end{table}

:::


### Exercises

5. Write the HF-HOME `ADSL` to a transport file without converting
   `TRT01P`, read it back, and show what happened to the
   treatment variable. Then fix the export so that the round trip
   preserves it.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
adsl_path <- file.path(xpt_dir, "adsl.xpt")

write_xpt(adsl, adsl_path, version = 5)
table(read_xpt(adsl_path)$TRT01P)
#> 
#>    1    2 
#> 1216 1216

write_xpt(mutate(adsl, TRT01P = as.character(TRT01P)), adsl_path,
          version = 5)
fixed <- read_xpt(adsl_path)
table(fixed$TRT01P)
#> 
#> Home health  Usual care 
#>        1216        1216
stopifnot(identical(sort(unique(fixed$TRT01P)), sort(arms)))
```
:::


The first export writes the factor's integer codes. The arms
therefore arrive as 1 and 2, with nothing to say which is which. A
SAS program that sets `ref = 'Usual care'` then fails to find the
level. One that does not set it silently uses 2 as the reference.
Converting to character writes the labels. In R, re-create the
factor with explicit levels after reading.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A SAS dataset arrives in R with a column `RANDDT`
whose values are around 23,400 and no format. What are the dates,
roughly, and how do you convert them?

**Answer.** Days since 1 January 1960, so about 64 years after
1960, in 2024. `as.Date(RANDDT, origin = "1960-01-01")` converts
them. Converting with R's default origin would place them in 2034,
ten years late. Every derived duration would still be right, which
is why the error survives until someone reads a date.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 8: a bug that produces a plausible number is the
   expensive kind.** Two languages that disagree by default both
   print a table; set every row of @tbl-sas-defaults explicitly
   before comparing.
2. **Habit 9: test the statistics, not the shape.** Equivalence
   means estimates that agree to several decimal places on the
   same data, and a disagreement is a default to find, not noise.
3. **Habit 6: count before and after every join.** Read the whole
   SAS log after every run; the MERGE repeats NOTE is a
   many-to-many join that did not warn you.

## Cumulative practice

6. *Cumulative (uses @sec-cdisc).* Write the HF-HOME `ADTTE` to a
   transport file, read it back, and refit the ITT Cox model on
   the file you read. Set every relevant row of @tbl-sas-defaults
   so that your R fit reproduces what the `PROC PHREG` program in
   @sec-sas-survival would compute, and write the SAS program
   that would confirm it.
7. *On your own work (no key).* If you have SAS access (ODA is
   enough), run that `PROC PHREG` program on your `adtte.xpt` and
   compare the hazard ratios with R's to four decimal places.
   Before you look, predict from @tbl-sas-defaults which numbers
   will differ if you remove `ties = efron`.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution to exercise 6'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
reread <- read_xpt(file.path(xpt_dir, "adtte.xpt")) |>
  mutate(TRT01P = factor(TRT01P, levels = arms),
         SEX    = factor(SEX, levels = c("F", "M"))) |>
  filter(ITTFL == "Y")

refit <- coxph(Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0) ~ TRT01P + AGE + SEX,
               data = reread, ties = "efron")
stopifnot(nrow(reread) == nrow(analysis),
          isTRUE(all.equal(coef(refit), coef(fit_cox))))
round(exp(cbind(HR = coef(refit), confint(refit))), 3)
#>                      HR 2.5 % 97.5 %
#> TRT01PHome health 0.847 0.712  1.008
#> AGE               1.020 1.012  1.028
#> SEXM              1.169 0.979  1.396
```
:::


Four rows matter here. The reference level is re-created as
`Usual care` after the round trip, matching `ref = 'Usual care'`.
`SEX` has reference `F` on both sides. The ties method is Efron,
stated in both. The censoring codes are `CNSR == 0` in R and
`cnsr(1 2)` in SAS. The SAS program is the `PROC PHREG` block of
@sec-sas-survival with `libname x xport` and `proc copy` in front
of it. The refit equals the original fit. That is the check that
the round trip lost nothing the model uses.
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Task | R | SAS |
|---|---|---|
| Read a CSV | `readr::read_csv("f.csv")` | `PROC IMPORT DATAFILE = 'f.csv' OUT = work.f DBMS = CSV;` |
| Keep rows | `filter(age >= 18)` | `if age >= 18;` (keeps missing `age`; add `not missing(age)`) |
| New variable | `mutate(log_bmi = log(bmi))` | `log_bmi = log(bmi);` in a DATA step |
| Running total | `mutate(total = cumsum(dose))` | `retain total 0; total = total + dose;` |
| Sort | `arrange(id, visit)` | `PROC SORT DATA = d; BY id visit;` |
| Join by key | `left_join(x, y, by = "id", relationship = "many-to-one")` | `MERGE x (IN = a) y; BY id; IF a;` after checking one row per `id` in `y` |
| Summarize by group | `group_by(g) \|> summarize(m = mean(x))` | `PROC MEANS; CLASS g; VAR x; OUTPUT OUT = s MEAN = m;` |
| Labels for codes | `factor(sex, 1:2, c("Male", "Female"))` | `PROC FORMAT; VALUE sexfmt 1 = 'Male' 2 = 'Female';` |
| Set the reference | `relevel(trt, ref = "Placebo")` | `CLASS trt (PARAM = REF REF = 'Placebo');` |
| Model `P(y = 1)` | `glm(y ~ x, family = binomial)` | `MODEL y (EVENT = '1') = x;` |
| ADaM survival | `Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0)` | `TIME aval*cnsr(1 2);` (every censoring code) |
| Cox ties | `coxph(..., ties = "efron")` (default) | `MODEL ... / TIES = EFRON;` |
| Write transport | `write_xpt(df, "f.xpt", version = 5)` | `LIBNAME x XPORT 'f.xpt'; PROC COPY IN = work OUT = x;` |
| Read transport | `read_xpt("f.xpt")` | `LIBNAME x XPORT 'f.xpt'; PROC COPY IN = x OUT = work;` |
| Bare SAS date | `as.Date(x, origin = "1960-01-01")` | Apply a format: `FORMAT x DATE9.;` |

: R to SAS at a glance. {#tbl-sas-cheat-sheet}

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-22}

1. A DATA step reads, creates, or transforms a SAS dataset row by
   row, using an implicit loop over records. PROC steps consume
   existing datasets and produce listings, tables, graphs, or
   statistical output. A PROC step does not create new
   observations (with rare exceptions). The typical workflow
   alternates: DATA step to shape the data, PROC step to analyze
   it.
2. In SAS, `PROC MEANS` or `PROC SUMMARY` produces analogous
   output (N, mean, SD, min, max, quantiles). In R, `summary(df)`
   gives a mixed-type summary across columns; `skimr::skim(df)` is
   closer to `PROC MEANS` output. `PROC UNIVARIATE` gives more
   detail (quantiles, skewness, kurtosis).
3. The SAS transport file (`.xpt`, SAS transport version 5) is
   the long-standing interchange format and is required for FDA
   submissions. In R, the `haven` package reads and writes `.xpt`
   and reads native `.sas7bdat`: `haven::read_xpt()`,
   `haven::write_xpt()`, `haven::read_sas()`.
